{PatientName}{PatientTitle}, the doctor just examined you and confirmed that you have cataracts. Have you noticed your vision looking hazy lately, like looking through frosted glass, or do lights seem to spread out and glare at night?

These are all typical symptoms of cataracts. Cataract surgery is currently the only effective way to improve vision. The procedure takes about 10 to 15 minutes, is usually done under local anesthesia, and you can return for a follow-up the next day. The surgical risk is relatively low, but complications such as infection, inflammation, or retinal detachment are still possible. After surgery, you'll need to follow your doctor's instructions, use eye drops on schedule, and avoid strenuous activity to help the wound heal. Next, I'll introduce you to lens surgery.

There are two main types of cataract surgery: phacoemulsification (ultrasound) and femtosecond laser-assisted surgery. The femtosecond laser can help complete some of the more delicate steps, such as the incision and pre-treatment of the lens, but both methods ultimately remove the cataract and insert an artificial lens using the same principle. Although the femtosecond laser offers higher precision, it is not covered by National Health Insurance and requires an out-of-pocket fee.

Before surgery, you'll need to decide whether to keep your nearsightedness. Everyday viewing distances can generally be divided into: far distance for driving and outdoor activities; medium distance, around 50–75 cm, for using a computer or cooking; and near distance, around 30 cm, for reading or using your phone. After cataract surgery, your eye will no longer have any focusing ability — instead, the power of the implanted lens determines which distance you can see clearly. If you choose a monofocal artificial lens, one focal range will be clearest, while the other two distances will require glasses. Choosing a multifocal lens means you won't need glasses and can adapt to different distances, but you should still watch for nighttime glare, and your eyes should be free of other conditions for the lens to work best.

Let me help you sort out the differences between the lens types. Simply put, an artificial lens is like buying glasses: a monofocal lens can only be set to see far 'or' near, while multifocal and trifocal lenses essentially build reading glasses right into your eye. An extended depth-of-focus lens lets you see the middle distance most naturally. These options differ quite a bit in terms of lifestyle fit and cost.

You can choose based on what you do most often in daily life. If you frequently cook, play cards, or use a computer, an extended depth-of-focus lens offers the most comfortable visual quality. If you'd like to see your phone and computer clearly without needing glasses, a trifocal or multifocal lens would be more convenient. Also, if you often drive at night, an aspheric or extended depth-of-focus lens is recommended, since they reduce nighttime glare and make the road safer to see. Now that you've heard all this, do you have a preference in mind?

Let me show you the estimated costs for surgery and lenses. National Health Insurance covers the most basic monofocal spherical lens, but it only provides clear distance vision — you'll still need glasses for near distance. A multifocal lens, which covers both near and far distance, costs about NT$60,000. An extended depth-of-focus lens for mid-to-far distance costs about NT$75,000. If you want to cover far, mid, and near distance vision all at once, you can choose a trifocal lens at your own expense, costing about NT$85,000 to NT$100,000. For patients with astigmatism, you can add an astigmatism-correcting option, such as toric or extended depth-of-focus toric lenses. Costs vary depending on the surgical method — femtosecond laser or ultrasound phacoemulsification — and the type of lens, so it's best to discuss the option that suits you with your attending physician.

Multifocal lenses may also cause some side effects after surgery. Some patients, especially at night, may notice halos spreading around lights, circular rings of light around a light source, or rays of light radiating outward. These effects vary from person to person, and most patients gradually adjust within 3 to 6 months. If you drive at night, it's recommended to discuss this thoroughly with your doctor before surgery to choose the lens best suited to your lifestyle.

v_str_Action: InsertAssitantMessage:Post-surgery care instructions for cataract surgery. Point 1: No eye drops are needed while the eye is covered with gauze. After surgery on the day of the procedure, your eye will be covered with gauze, so no eye drops are needed that day — just start using the eye drops at the time your doctor instructs. Point 2: Bring the medications prescribed on the day of surgery to your follow-up visit. At your follow-up visit the next day, please bring the medications your doctor prescribed on the day of surgery, such as eye drops, ointment, an eye shield, or a care kit, so the doctor can check them before you start using the eye drops as instructed. Point 3: Light sensitivity, tearing, and mild localized stinging are normal. If you feel more sensitive to light, have tearing, or experience mild stinging in your eye after surgery, these are actually normal post-surgery symptoms. As long as you follow your doctor's care instructions, these symptoms will usually gradually improve, so there's no need to worry too much. Point 4: If you experience any discomfort, return to the clinic or go to the emergency room right away. If after surgery you notice a sudden, significant decrease in vision, unusual pain, redness, heavy bleeding, or abnormal discharge, please return to the clinic or go to the emergency room for treatment immediately. Point 5: Rest in bed as much as possible and avoid risky movements. On the day of surgery, please rest in bed as much as possible and avoid any risky movements that could put pressure on the eye, such as coughing forcefully, bending over, lifting heavy objects, or strenuous exercise, to avoid affecting wound healing. Point 6: Maintain a regular routine and take your medications on schedule. Please maintain a regular daily routine after surgery, keep your schedule stable, avoid overexertion, and take all prescribed medications on schedule as instructed by your doctor. Point 7: Avoid getting water in your eye, and avoid swimming and strenuous exercise for one month. Within one month after surgery, please avoid letting your eye come into contact with water, and avoid swimming and any strenuous exercise, to ensure the safety of your eye. Point 8: Wear the eye shield for one month, both day and night. Within one month after surgery, please wear the eye shield all day, every day, including while sleeping, to ensure the safety and protection of your eye.
